items.title: Nvidia's six-week losing streak, its longest since 2012, goes into earnings without its CEO
items.idea: Jensen Huang resigned as CEO and director Thursday, and CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO. NVDA lost 12.8% on the week, a sixth straight weekly decline and the longest streak since 2012, and closed below $4T for the first time since July 2025. AMD (+18.9%), AVGO (+18.2%) and MU (+12.8%) caught the rotation. Earnings come Tue Nov 17 on a $108B ±2% guide that assumes zero China data center revenue.
items.angle: The print is now a governance event as much as a numbers event. A beat with no CEO may not re-rate the stock, while AMD/AVGO already carry the 'share shift' premium.
items.tweetA: AMD +19%, AVGO +18%, NVDA -13% in one week. The market has already decided where the share goes after Jensen leaves. Tuesday's print has to prove the order book doesn't follow the founder. $NVDA $AMD $AVGO
items.tweetB: The guide assumes zero China data center revenue, so the China risk is already out of the numbers. What isn't priced is a CFO acting as interim CEO answering roadmap questions on the call. Watch the Rubin cadence language, not the EPS line.

items.title: Bernstein halves its NVDA target to $200; a short seller says >20% of compute revenue was China-driven
items.idea: Bernstein cut its target from $400 to $200, Wedbush went from $300 to $225 and Oppenheimer pulled its target. TechCrunch put peak-to-trough losses at up to 19%, or $855B+ of market value. Culper Research (short) estimates more than 20% of Nvidia's FY26 compute revenue was ultimately driven by Chinese demand. Nvidia says inspections found no chip diversion. Singapore's probe of the Megaspeed executive concerned false server-purchase declarations, not espionage.
items.angle: Halving a target on a governance event is unusual. It suggests the sell side is repricing the multiple (key-person plus export-control risk), not cutting estimates.
items.tweetA: Bernstein halved its $NVDA target without touching revenue estimates. That's a multiple call: the market now applies a key-person discount to the world's most important chip company. Key-person discounts usually don't come off quickly.
items.tweetB: If Culper is even half right that 20% of compute demand was China-routed, the 'zero China' guide isn't conservative. It's the new base. The Megaspeed/Singapore trail matters more for export-control policy than for the affair headlines.

items.title: PPI +6.5% y/y is the hottest since Nov 2022, and BLS can't publish annual CPI
items.idea: October CPI rose 0.4% (0.3% expected), and core rose 0.3% for a third straight month. BLS published no annual CPI rate because the 2025 shutdown left no October 2025 baseline. PPI rose 6.5% y/y, the largest gain since Nov 2022. The 10Y closed near 5.13% (+27bp on the week), the 2Y had its biggest weekly jump in 2+ years, and DXY hit its highest since April 2025. Goldman added a March hike.
items.angle: With no official y/y CPI, PPI and PCE become the headline inflation prints, and PPI at 6.5% is the scarier one. Pipeline pressure argues against Rosenberg's view that commodity prices are already 20% off their peaks.
items.tweetA: The BLS can't tell you annual CPI because the 2025 shutdown erased the baseline. So the headline inflation number this month is PPI at +6.5% y/y. That's the print the Fed is reacting to, and it's the worst since 2022.
items.tweetB: Core CPI at 0.3% for three straight months annualizes to ~3.7%. Goldman just added a March hike. The question is no longer whether the Fed hikes in December but whether it's the last hike, and history says that's what decides the equity outcome.

items.title: Boockvar: if AI capex breaks, the deficit goes from 6% to 12% of GDP
items.idea: Boockvar thinks 10Y yields have seen a short-term peak (5.30% high, then 4.85%) but long-end rates will trend higher for years. He expects the ECB, BoE and BoJ to hike in December. AI capex peaks in 2027 in both dollars and rate of change. A capex slowdown ends Fed hikes, but a resulting recession would push the deficit from 6% to 12% of GDP and flood the market with Treasuries. About a third of his portfolio is commodity equities (energy, fertilizer, precious metals, uranium). Central banks bought ~320t of gold in Q3.
items.angle: This is the trap for bond bulls: the scenario that ends the hikes (an AI bust) is also the scenario that doubles supply. The curve steepens either way.
items.tweetA: Boockvar's trap: AI capex keeps going and the Fed keeps hiking, or AI capex breaks, the deficit doubles to 12% of GDP and term premium explodes. Either way the long end loses. Steepeners are the only thing that wins both. $TLT $TBT
items.tweetB: A December hike by the ECB, BoE, BoJ and Fed at the same time would be the first globally synchronized tightening since 2022, landing on top of a Nasdaq that's already liquidating.

items.tweetB: Levin's twist: if a lab nears a $30T TAM, it gets nationalized first. That caps the upside on frontier-lab equity in a way no IPO prospectus will mention, just before the Anthropic pricing.

items.tweetB: Central banks bought 320 tonnes in Q3 while gold had its worst week since June. Official buyers are price-insensitive and leveraged traders are forced sellers. That split is usually how a bottom forms.

items.title: Goldman's China profit paradox: capital so cheap it destroys returns
items.idea: China added ~$5T to its economy since the pandemic and leads in EVs, batteries, robotics and AI, yet equity holders have little to show. Goldman's Kinger Lau and Timothy Moe argue the root cause is deeper than deflation or price wars: the cost of capital is so low, and policy so tilted to production, that companies can keep expanding capacity without earning attractive returns. Goldman's 5-year EPS projections require meaningful improvement, and upside is concentrated in a small group of cash-generating, structural-growth names.
items.angle: This is the mirror image of the US AI-capex debate. Cheap capital plus a strategic mandate produces overcapacity and poor ROIC. US hyperscalers funded by SPVs and vendor financing are drifting toward the same model.
items.tweetA: China proves you can win the industry and lose the shareholder. $5T of GDP growth, global dominance in EVs and batteries, and miserable equity returns, because capital was too cheap to force discipline. Now look at US AI capex funded by SPVs and vendor loans.
items.tweetB: Goldman's China fix is to own the few companies that escape the capacity trap. That's also the right AI framework for 2027: the winners are the ones with pricing power over their own buyers, not the ones building the most. $BABA $TCEHY

items.title: Core CPI landed exactly on Waller's 50bp line, and Kalshi's 50bp odds more than doubled
items.idea: Hours before CPI, Waller said core ≥0.3% puts a 50bp hike on the table and anything smaller risks credibility. Core printed exactly 0.3%. Kalshi for Dec 9: 25bp 82% (from 88%), 50bp 12% (from 5%), hold 4% (from 8%). The context: core PCE 3.1%, payrolls 165K vs 65K expected, September PPI +1.3% m/m, and two FOMC dissents for a hike in October. Hike analogs one year later: Feb 1995 S&P +35%, May 2000 -12% (Nasdaq -45%), May 2022 -5%, Dec 2022 +18%.
items.angle: The analogs split on one variable: whether it's the last hike and whether earnings are rolling over. Last hike plus healthy earnings (1995, Dec 2022) gave big gains. Last hike plus peaking earnings (2000) gave a crash.
items.tweetA: Four hiking analogs: 1995 +35%, Dec 2022 +18%, May 2022 -5%, 2000 -12% (Nasdaq -45%). The difference is earnings momentum, not the size of the hike. If AI capex peaks in 2027 as the Street now says, December 2026 rhymes with May 2000.
items.tweetB: Waller set the 50bp trigger at core 0.3%, and it printed 0.3% to the decimal. Kalshi 50bp odds went 5%→12% in a day. When a governor publicly pre-commits, the market's job is to call the bluff. Watch the minutes on the 18th.

items.title: Rate expectations across 8 economies swung ~175bp in two years: from -125bp to +50bp
items.idea: A Bloomberg chart averages the 12-month priced policy-rate change across 8 economies. In autumn 2024 it priced ~125bp of cuts. It was ~-10bp at the start of 2026, went vertical after the US/Israel strikes on Iran, hit ~+80bp during the French risk-premium spike, cooled to +33bp on Nov 6 and is back above +50bp after CPI. The 2Y rose 30bp in 2 sessions to 4.89%, its biggest 2-day jump since March 2023. Every time the 10Y jumped >100bp in a few months (1994, 2013, 2022, 2023), stocks paid 6-25%.
items.angle: A global hiking impulse, not just a Fed one, is why the dollar can rally even with Fed hikes priced. It also hits EM and Europe through the currency channel.
items.tweetA: From 125bp of global cuts priced to 50bp of global hikes priced in two years. A 175bp swing in the world's expected policy rate, and equity multiples are within 5% of the highs. Something has to give, and history says it's the multiple.
items.tweetB: 1994: 10Y +280bp, S&P -9%, peso -50%. 2013: +140bp, rupee -20%. The equity hit from a bond rout gets exported to EM currencies. Japanese and Australian yields at multi-year highs say the export has already started. $EEM

items.title: MSCI removes Strategy from the USA Index on Nov 30 under a new 'non-operating company' screen
items.idea: MSCI's November review removes Strategy (MSTR) from the MSCI USA Index at the Nov 30 close, and Metaplanet leaves MSCI Japan Small Cap the same day. They're among the first six cuts under a new screen that tests how much of a company's assets are actually used to run a business. Unlike the 23 other USA deletions, they don't migrate to small cap. Strategy puts MSCI-tracking stakes at ~13M shares (3.1% of basic shares). JPMorgan's old estimate was ~$2.8B of outflows.
items.angle: A defined, dated forced-selling event. More importantly, the 'non-operating' screen sets a precedent other index providers (FTSE, S&P) could copy, which threatens the whole BTC-treasury-company model.

items.title: Ledger's SDK phones home every signature by default, a month after a $100M device attack
items.idea: Ambire developer Kaloyan Kosev says Ledger's SDK reports every signature to Ledger by default: network, destination address, device, firmware and whether the user blind-signed. Ambire disabled it in September. Ledger's Donjon says it's part of Clear Signing (the metadata files are too big for the device), Ledger doesn't keep the data, and wallets can swap modules. It follows a supply-chain attack that drained ~$100M from tampered Ledger devices last month.
items.angle: Self-custody's privacy promise depends on middleware few users audit. The data set (address + device + blind-sign flag) is exactly what a targeted attacker wants.
items.tweetA: A hardware wallet that reports every destination address and whether you blind-signed is a targeting database, whether or not Ledger keeps it. After a $100M supply-chain drain, 'trust us, we delete it' isn't a security model.
items.tweetB: Self-custody's weakest link is the SDK nobody reads, not the chip. This is the crypto version of the 2024 xz backdoor lesson: the attack surface is the dependency tree.

items.tweetB: FaceStealer: hijack a friend's account, replay their stolen webcam on a video call, fake a glitch, install malware. $400M in 18 months. Video calls can no longer verify identity, and banks still treat them as KYC.

items.title: The yen has a flow problem: NISA sent $194B unhedged into foreign equities, so rate spreads say 140 while spot is 160
items.idea: MUFG (Halpenny, Hardman, Lockhart): the 5-year US-Japan 2Y spread relationship implies USD/JPY near 140, not 160. The gap comes from household flows: since NISA allowances tripled in Jan 2024, investment trusts bought ~¥29.7T (~$194B) of foreign equities, mostly unhedged. Japanese households still hold 47.2% of financial assets in cash and deposits (US 10.7%, euro area 31.1%), or ~¥1,126T ($7T). MUFG sees intervention somewhere between here and ~164.
items.angle: Moving Japan's cash share to the euro-area mix would free ~¥380T (~$2.4T). Where that goes, home or abroad, is the biggest structural FX question in G10.
items.tweetA: Japanese households hold 47% of their wealth in cash. Moving to the euro-area mix (31%) frees ~¥380T, about $2.4T. NISA has sent $194B of it abroad unhedged so far. That's why USD/JPY ignores rate spreads, and why intervention alone can't fix it. $FXY
items.tweetB: The rate spread says USD/JPY should be 140, and spot is 160. A 20-figure gap from retail flows is a reflexive bubble in reverse. When NISA money starts staying home (JGBs to retail just hit a record), the snap-back won't be gradual.
